citation: 32 CFR § 117.10, Determination of eligibility for access to classified information (National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual rule). Read on law.cornell.edu.

publisher: Department of Defense (Legal Information Institute mirror of the e-CFR)
population: contractors in the National Industrial Security Program
effect: eligibility requested only where access is essential to a classified contract, for the minimum number of employees, never to build a cache (§117.10(a)(1), (a)(5)); not for non-employees or subcontractor employees (a)(7); pre-employment investigation allowed with a written commitment accepted in writing, employment to begin within 45 days of the eligibility grant (f); temporary eligibility only with no adverse information, not beyond one year without CSA approval, valid at level but not for RD, COMSEC or NATO until final, withdrawal not appealable, non-U.S. citizens ineligible (l); reciprocity under SEAD 7 (a)(6), (h); access restored after a break in employment without a new investigation if eligibility continued (i), (j); denial, suspension or revocation means immediate removal from access (a)(2); non-U.S. citizens only by Limited Access Authorization in rare cases, never for Top Secret, RD, COMSEC, intelligence or NATO (k)
summary: The rule that fixes who a contractor can get cleared and when. A clearance request needs a classified contract the person will work on, is limited to the minimum number of people, and may not be used to build a bench; a candidate can be investigated before employment only on a written commitment and must start within 45 days of the grant. Temporary (interim) eligibility exists but only where nothing adverse has surfaced, and its withdrawal cannot be appealed. A non-citizen can be cleared only by a Limited Access Authorization in rare cases.
why_it_mattered: The rule that decides who a contractor can get cleared and when: a contract need, no bench, a written commitment before employment and a start within 45 days of the grant; the clear-start stage is built on it.
key_facts: Requests "will not be used to establish a cache of cleared employees" (§117.10(a)(5))
Pre-employment request: written commitment, accepted in writing; employment must begin within 45 days of the grant (§117.10(f))
Temporary eligibility: no adverse information; up to one year; not valid for RD, COMSEC, NATO until final; withdrawal not appealable (§117.10(l))
Limited Access Authorization for non-U.S. citizens only with unique or urgently needed skills and no clearable citizen available (§117.10(k))

citation: Speer, A. B., Hardy, J. H., III, Gibson, C., Frost, C., & Hong, Q. (2026). Now you see them, now you don't: Understanding new hire ghosting and its antecedents. Human Resource Management Journal. Read on a publisher-permitted copy hosted by HireVue.
population: Study 1: 157,154 accepted entry-level offers at one large U.S./Canadian telecommunications company, May 2019–June 2025 (HRIS records); Study 2: 434 U.S. adults (205 recent ghosters, 229 non-ghosters) from a Prolific screen of 9,040
effect: ghosting rate 4.1% of accepted offers (peak 6.1% in April 2020); each additional week between offer acceptance and start date raised the odds of ghosting (b = 0.20, OR = 1.22, r = .11); employee referral OR 0.42; company communication quality OR 0.56; organizational attractiveness OR 0.57; financial security OR 0.86; external offers OR 1.18; impulsivity OR 2.05 (1.69 in the full model); reasons given by ghosters: alternate job 39%, pay 29%, negative company perception 24%, the work 23%, family or scheduling 17%, communication 14%
summary: The only field evidence found on what happens between acceptance and the first day. Among 157,154 accepted entry-level offers at one telecom employer, 4.1 percent never showed, and every extra week of waiting raised the odds by about a fifth. The survey study adds the protective factors: a referral, good communication from the company, attraction to the firm and financial security, against a competing offer and impulsivity. The population is entry-level and customer-facing, not cleared technical staff, so the rates do not transfer; the mechanism is what the pack carries.
key_facts: Each additional week from acceptance to start: OR 1.22 for ghosting (N = 157,154)
Referral OR 0.42; communication quality OR 0.56; financial security OR 0.86; external offers OR 1.18
Ghosters' reasons: alternate job 39%, pay 29%, company perception 24%
quotes: Hires with longer offer-to-start delays and customer-facing roles experienced greater ghosting risk.

citation: Bauer, T. N., Erdogan, B., Ellis, A. M., Truxillo, D. M., Brady, G. M., & Bodner, T. (2025). New horizons for newcomer organizational socialization: A review, meta-analysis, and future research directions. Journal of Management, 51(1), 344–382. Read on the University of Exeter repository copy.
publisher: SAGE (author manuscript on the Exeter repository)
population: 256 eligible studies, 183 samples meta-analysed; newcomers with twelve months' tenure or less; mean age 28.4; 53% male
effect: institutionalized socialization tactics r = .24 to .40 with social acceptance, role clarity, task mastery and fit; social tactics .29 to .47 (strongest), content tactics up to .43 (role clarity), context tactics .10 to .30; newcomer information seeking .19 to .25, feedback seeking .21 to .32, relationship building .20 to .31, positive framing .39 to .49; social acceptance → job satisfaction .42, commitment .40, performance .35, turnover intentions −.27, turnover −.12, well-being .31; role clarity → satisfaction .38, commitment .33, performance .23, turnover −.09; task mastery → performance .38; perceived fit → satisfaction .46, turnover intentions −.31; mentoring related to role clarity more strongly in horizontal-individualistic cultures (.38 vs .17)
summary: The current meta-analysis of newcomer socialization, which supersedes the 2007 review it extends. Structured, institutionalized onboarding and the newcomer's own proactive behaviour both predict adjustment, social acceptance is the strongest and most consistent path to the outcomes a firm cares about, and the links from adjustment to actual turnover are small (about −.1) while the links to satisfaction, commitment and performance are moderate. Insider mentoring and support appear central. The authors flag perceived fit as under-studied and well-being as an outcome.
why_it_mattered: The current meta-analysis of newcomer socialization: structured onboarding and the newcomer's own proactivity predict adjustment, and social acceptance is the strongest path to the outcomes a firm cares about.
key_facts: Social tactics (insiders, mentoring, investiture) r .29–.47 with adjustment; institutionalized tactics .24–.40
Social acceptance → performance .35, turnover intentions −.27, turnover −.12
Positive framing by the newcomer .39–.49 with adjustment; information seeking .19–.25
quotes: The effective socialization of newcomers into organizations is critical for employee and organizational success.

citation: Bauer, T. N., Bodner, T., Erdogan, B., Truxillo, D. M., & Tucker, J. S. (2007). Newcomer adjustment during organizational socialization: A meta-analytic review of antecedents, outcomes, and methods. Journal of Applied Psychology, 92(3), 707–721.

effect: role clarity, self-efficacy and social acceptance mediated the effects of socialization tactics and information seeking on job satisfaction, organizational commitment, job performance, intentions to remain and turnover; the model was generally supported; methods (longitudinal vs cross-sectional; school-to-work vs work-to-work) moderated some relationships
summary: The 2007 meta-analysis that set the three-mediator model of newcomer adjustment the 2025 review extends; read from the abstract for the model and the sample count, with the effect sizes taken from the 2025 update.
key_facts: 70 samples; adjustment (role clarity, self-efficacy, social acceptance) mediates tactics → outcomes

citation: Allen, D. G. (2006). Do organizational socialization tactics influence newcomer embeddedness and turnover? Journal of Management, 32(2), 237–256. Read on a university course mirror.
population: 222 newcomers at one large U.S. financial-services organization with no standardized orientation; 82 cities; turnover tracked one year
effect: 24.8% voluntary turnover within a year; investiture tactics (OR 0.52) and serial tactics, meaning experienced insiders as role models (OR 0.44), predicted lower turnover; collective, investiture and fixed tactics predicted on-the-job embeddedness (β .22, .38, .21); on-the-job embeddedness predicted lower turnover (OR 0.42) and partly mediated the investiture effect
summary: A one-firm prospective test of which onboarding tactics keep people: having experienced insiders as guides and affirming who the newcomer already is each roughly halved the odds of leaving within the year, and the mechanism ran through how embedded the newcomer became in the job. One firm, mostly non-technical staff; the direction is what carries.
key_facts: Serial tactics OR 0.44; investiture OR 0.52 for turnover within a year (N = 222)
On-the-job embeddedness OR 0.42 for turnover; off-the-job embeddedness not significant
quotes: on-the-job embeddedness is negatively related to turnover

citation: Kammeyer-Mueller, J., Wanberg, C., Rubenstein, A., & Song, Z. (2013). Support, undermining, and newcomer socialization: Fitting in during the first 90 days. Academy of Management Journal, 56(4), 1104–1124. Read on the Carlson School copy.
population: 264 new hires at one research university (255 completed all 14 weekly waves); research specialists, technicians, advisors, coordinators, accountants; 49.8% with graduate degrees
effect: supervisor support, coworker support and hedonic tone declined significantly over the first 14 weeks; early support and undermining predicted 90-day outcomes more than their trajectories did; proactive behaviour partly mediated support → outcomes; supervisor undermining raised the turnover hazard (HR 3.01)
summary: Fourteen weekly surveys of the first ninety days: the support a newcomer gets from the supervisor and the team falls off week by week, what they got at the start predicts how integrated and committed they are at ninety days, and a supervisor who undermines them triples the hazard of leaving. One university's professional and technical staff.
key_facts: Support declines over the first 14 weeks; early support predicts 90-day integration and commitment
Supervisor undermining HR 3.01 for turnover
quotes: Supervisor undermining was uniquely associated with higher turnover (exit) hazard.

summary: The cleanest measurement of a new hire's ramp: output rose by half in the first year on a job where output is counted per worker, pay rose much less, and the people who stayed were the ones who learned fastest. The job is manual, not technical, so the slope does not transfer; the shape and the pay–output gap do.
key_facts: Output 53% higher after one year than at hire
Pay profiles much flatter than output profiles in the first 18 months
quotes: output is 53 percent higher after one year than it is initially when hired

citation: Acemoglu, D., & Pischke, J.-S. (1998). Why do firms train? Theory and evidence. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 113(1), 79–119.
population: German apprentices (microdata)
effect: a theory in which workers do not pay for the general training they receive: the current employer's superior information about the worker's ability creates ex post monopsony power that makes it worth paying for general skills; multiple equilibria (low training and high quits, or high training and low quits); German apprentice data give the predictions some support
summary: The reason firms pay for skills that walk: the employer who trained someone knows what they can do better than the market does, and that information advantage lets it keep part of the return. The pack carries the mechanism; the Becker baseline that workers pay for general training is stated against it. Read from the abstract.
why_it_mattered: The reason firms pay for skills that walk: the employer who trained someone knows more about them than the market does and keeps part of the return, which turns training from a cost into a bet the develop stage prices.
key_facts: Employer's informational advantage → ex post monopsony → pays for general training
quotes: This paper offers a theory of training whereby workers do not pay for the general training they receive.
role_note: why a small firm trains at all

It carries the meta-analytic numbers from Blume et al. and Colquitt et al.; the Blume meta-analysis itself is a todo. The "10 percent transfers" figure is a 1982 estimate the review repeats, not a measurement.
key_facts: Supervisor support ρ .31 vs peer support .14 with transfer (Blume et al. 2010)
Transfer climate .37; cognitive ability .43 (Colquitt et al. 2000)
Realistic training environments, behavioural modelling, error management, opportunity to perform
quotes: motivation to transfer exhibited a markedly stronger relationship with transfer (0.43) than did motivation to learn (0.07)

summary: The plain-language companion to the transfer literature, cited for framing and for the open- versus closed-skill distinction; it carries no effect sizes.
key_facts: Open skills (flexible performance) depend more on motivation and self-efficacy than closed skills

quotes: it is outside normal hours, it is voluntary, not job related, and no other work is concurrently performed.

citation: Rubenstein, A. L., Eberly, M. B., Lee, T. W., & Mitchell, T. R. (2018). Surveying the forest: A meta-analysis, moderator investigation, and future-oriented discussion of the antecedents of voluntary employee turnover. Personnel Psychology, 71(1), 23–65. Read on a mirror of the accepted manuscript.
population: 316 articles, 57 predictors, about 1,800 effect sizes; mean sample 1,053; 78.9% U.S. samples; healthcare 25.9%, banking 12.6%; mean lag about 16 months
effect: corrected correlations with voluntary turnover: withdrawal cognitions .56 (k = 211); job search .40 (k = 27); organizational commitment −.29 (k = 129); person–job/organization fit −.29 (k = 17); job satisfaction −.28 (k = 174); job embeddedness −.26 (k = 29); leadership including LMX −.24 (k = 42); climate −.24 (k = 8); perceived alternatives .23 (k = 79); stress and exhaustion .21 (k = 32); age −.21 (k = 121); tenure −.20 (k = 118); engagement −.20 (k = 4); work–life conflict .19 (k = 7); pay −.17 (k = 55); role ambiguity and role conflict .15 each; coworker support −.14 (k = 24); workload −.10 (k = 21); performance −.08 (k = 86), −.21 with an outlier removed; age and satisfaction matter more where base rates are higher; alternatives matter more where withdrawal cognitions are high
summary: The current map of why people quit, 316 studies and 57 predictors deep. Wanting to leave and looking are the strongest signals, then commitment, fit, satisfaction and embeddedness in a cluster near −.3, then the supervisor, the climate and the outside alternatives near ±.24. Pay is real but modest at −.17, workload barely registers, and stress and work–life conflict sit around .2. Mostly U.S., healthcare-heavy; read to the end of the predictor table.
why_it_mattered: The current map of why people quit across 316 studies: wanting to leave and looking come first, attitudes and embeddedness next, pay well down the list; the retain stage is ordered by this table.
key_facts: Withdrawal cognitions ρ .56; job search .40; commitment −.29; satisfaction −.28; embeddedness −.26; leadership −.24; alternatives .23; pay −.17
Stress .21; work–life conflict .19; workload −.10; performance −.08 (−.21 without an outlier)
quotes: mean time lag between predictor and turnover measurement was roughly 16 months

Firm-specific training −.40, internal mobility −.25, staffing selectivity −.24; general training, staffing levels and straight pay n.s.

citation: Dube, A., Giuliano, L., & Leonard, J. (2019). Fairness and frictions: The impact of unequal raises on quit behavior. American Economic Review, 109(2), 620–663.

why_it_mattered: The cleanest evidence that people leave over what the person next to them got, not over the market, which is the peer mechanism behind the pay-review lever and the compression constraint.
key_facts: Own-wage effects on quits mostly reflect comparisons with higher-paid peers
Separations fairly insensitive when raises are similar across peers
quotes: The peer effect is driven by comparisons with higher-paid peers—suggesting concerns about fairness.

citation: Federal Acquisition Regulation 37.104, Personal services contracts. acquisition.gov, FAC 2026-01.
date_note: current text as of access
population: federal service contracts and the contractor personnel performing them
effect: a personal services contract is characterized by the employer-employee relationship it creates between the government and the contractor's personnel (a); agencies shall not award one unless specifically authorized by statute (b); the relationship arises when contractor personnel are subject to the relatively continuous supervision and control of a government officer or employee, and giving orders for a specific result with the right to reject the product does not by itself create it (c); the descriptive elements: performance on site, government-furnished tools and equipment, services applied directly to the agency's integral effort, comparable civil-service work, a need lasting beyond one year, and a nature requiring government direction (d)
summary: The rule that bounds how far a customer may run the firm''s people: the government may specify the result and reject the product, and may set the qualifications the contract requires, but may not supervise and control the contractor''s employees as if they were its own, which is what a customer that picks, directs and rates individual staff is drifting toward. For a small firm it is both a limit on the customer and a reason the customer''s approval of a candidate is framed as a contract requirement rather than a hiring decision (synthesis).
key_facts: Personal services contracts barred absent statute (b); the key question is relatively continuous supervision and control (c)
Six descriptive elements (d): on site, government tools, integral effort, comparable civil-service work, beyond one year, needs direction
quotes: the key question always being: Will the Government exercise relatively continuous supervision and control
role_note: the limit on customer direction of contractor staff
